sentence: A 74-year-old female patient who came to the emergency room after having suffered accidental blunt trauma at home, of moderate intensity to the left eye (LE), when she hit the edge of the nightstand.
Her history included mild ametropia without optical correction and type 2 diabetes mellitus being treated with oral antidiabetics.
She did not have any other personal or family history of interest.
Her visual acuity (VA) was 0.6 in the right eye and light perception did not improve with pinhole vision in the LE.

The slit lamp examination revealed hematoma and edema in the left upper eyelid, intact conjunctiva with intense generalized chemosis, intact and transparent cornea, and 100% hyphema that prevented assessment of the rest of the ocular structures.
Hypotonia of the LE was observed with an intraocular pressure of 5 mm Hg.

Imaging tests were performed (computed tomography and magnetic resonance imaging) showing the existence of a superior nasal paralimbar scleral incised wound of approximately 10 mm and the presence of an intact lens prolapsed into the subconjunctival space.
The conjunctival chemosis quickly evolved into generalized hyposphagma, allowing us to appreciate the existence of a superior nasal subconjunctival mass that corresponded to the prolapsed lens.
The patient underwent surgery, performing a 360º peritomy, extraction of the prolapsed lens, suturing of the scleral wound, and treatment with reinforced intravenous and topical antibiotic therapy.
One month after surgery, the patient had hand movement VA that improved to 0.1 with a correction of + 14.00 diopters.
The slit lamp showed a transparent cornea, superior nasal corectopia with loss of iridian tissue and adhered debris.
The fundus, which could not be seen due to media opacity, showed retina in situ on the B-mode ultrasound.
At twelve months, a combined surgery of vitrectomy via pars plana and suturing of the intraocular lens to the sulcus was performed, achieving a spontaneous VA of 0.3 at eighteen months.
